title: Recovery sprint + AKS/GitOps capstones
subtitle: R1–R6: 8-hour Azure and CI/CD recovery · R7: Kubernetes/AKS · R8: GitOps/Argo CD and production API delivery
intro: R1–R6 retain the original two-day, eight-hour recovery sprint. R7 and R8 extend it with two two-hour capstones, splittable into shorter sessions. Every block starts with recall from memory, then guided-to-solo practice, evidence and a 60–90 second English explanation. Solutions remain sealed until an attempt is recorded. Time does not prove completion. No paid resources are created without explicit approval.
rules: Answer the recall questions before reading the instructions. "I don't remember" is a valid answer and is exactly what the sprint is for.

Record your attempt before opening a solution. Every hint or solution opened before completion makes the block AI-assisted. Break/fix steps are optional: a quick extra, not needed to complete the block — incidents come after the sprint.
Automatic checks only read Azure, GitHub and local files. Nothing in the sprint deploys, destroys or changes permissions; steps that take a lease or need an OK say so.
When the environment or a tool blocks you, report it as a blocker. It is not counted as a technical mistake.
Completing a sprint block does not complete a platform session or an AZ-400 lab: those keep their own checkers and Validate.ps1.
R7 and R8 reuse the existing customer portal, 40-aks layer and GitOps files. A local Helm render is not proof of an AKS deployment.
An HTTP API endpoint, the Kubernetes API server endpoint and an Azure Private Endpoint are distinct; trace all three where relevant.

blocks.title: Diagnosis and current state
blocks.focus: Active recall, environment inventory, gap list
blocks.objective: Find out, without notes, what you still remember about this platform; inventory what is really deployed; and write the gap list that steers the next five blocks.
blocks.interviewAngle: Clients open with "walk me through the platform you operate". You need the layers, what is deployed and why, in your own words.

prerequisites.notes: Signed in with az login on the lab subscription and gh auth login. No layer needs to be applied for this block.

reuse.note: Lab 00 (sandbox bootstrap) and session C001 are already verified; their evidence shows the tools and the subscription worked then. This block checks they still work today.

recall.question: Without opening the repository: which Terraform layers does the platform have (00 → 70), what does each one own, and which are deployed today?
recall.answer: 00-bootstrap (state storage), 05-identity (OIDC app registrations, RBAC), 10-foundation (hub & spoke, NSG, private DNS zones, Log Analytics, Managed Prometheus), 20-governance (Azure Policy, Defender), 30-data (SQL, Key Vault, private endpoints), 40-aks, 50-edge (Front Door, WAF, DNS, Traffic Manager), 60-observability, 70-datadog. Deployed: 00, 05, 10, 20.

recall.question: Where does each layer keep its Terraform state, and how does a pipeline sign in to Azure without a stored secret?
recall.answer: One blob per layer (<layer>.tfstate) in the tfstate container of a storage account in rg-mfs-tfstate, accessed with Entra ID (shared keys disabled). Pipelines use OIDC / workload identity federation: the CI platform issues a short-lived token and Entra exchanges it because a federated credential trusts that exact issuer + subject.

recall.question: In GitHub Actions and in Azure Pipelines: what is the difference between a job, a stage and an environment?
recall.answer: A job is a set of steps on one runner/agent. Azure Pipelines groups jobs into stages (GitHub has no stages; jobs are chained with needs). An environment is a deployment target with protection: approvals/required reviewers, branch rules, checks — and in GitHub it also changes the OIDC subject.

recall.question: A terraform plan fails in CI. Name the first three things you check.
recall.answer: 1) The failing step and its exact error (auth, backend/state, provider, code). 2) Identity: which principal, which subject/service connection, does it have RBAC on the subscription and on the state storage. 3) What changed: the commit, variables, provider versions, a lock left behind or drift.

steps.title: Check tools and sign-ins
steps.detail: Before trusting any evidence, prove the tools and identities you will use today. Read each line of output and say which account and subscription you are on.
steps.command:
az version --query '"azure-cli"'; terraform version; gh auth status; git --version
az account show --query "{subscription:name, id:id, user:user.name}" -o table
hints: Which line tells you the Azure subscription, and is it the lab one?
gh auth status shows the account and the token scopes; you need repo access to edymonte/azure-enterprise-platform.
steps.solution: Expected: Azure CLI 2.x, Terraform 1.12.x, gh signed in as edymonte, subscription "sub-mfs-platform-lab" (26e19954-…). If az account show fails: az login; if the subscription is wrong: az account set --subscription <id>. A wrong subscription is an environment blocker, not a technical mistake.

steps.title: Inventory the deployed layers
steps.detail: azp.ps1 status reads each layer's state and tells you what exists. Predict the result before you run it.
steps.command: ./scripts/azp.ps1 status
hints: Which layers would you expect to see with resources, given the sessions you have done?
A layer with no state blob was never applied.
steps.solution: Expected: 00-bootstrap, 05-identity, 10-foundation and 20-governance have resources; 30-data, 40-aks, 50-edge, 60-observability and 70-datadog do not. This is the baseline for every interview answer: say what is deployed and what is only code.

steps.title: Map resource groups to layers
steps.detail: List the platform resource groups yourself (they all start with rg-mfs) and write, for each one, which layer created it and what lives there. Only the start of the command is given.
steps.command: az group list --query "[?starts_with(name, 'rg-mfs')]..."
hints: A JMESPath projection like .{rg:name, location:location} gives you a readable table.
rg-mfs-tfstate is 00-bootstrap; the other three come from 10-foundation and 50-edge (DNS zone).
steps.solution: az group list --query "[?starts_with(name, 'rg-mfs')].{rg:name, location:location}" -o table → rg-mfs-tfstate (00-bootstrap: state storage), rg-mfs-hub-lab (10-foundation: hub VNet, private DNS zones, Log Analytics, Azure Monitor workspace), rg-mfs-portal-lab (10-foundation: spoke VNet, AKS subnet, NSG; later SQL/AKS), rg-mfs-dns (public zone edymonte.com.br).

steps.title: Write your gap list
steps.detail: Rate yourself 0 (can't do it), 1 (with notes) or 2 (could explain it to a client) on: VNet peering, NSG, private DNS, RBAC data vs control plane, Terraform state, locking, drift, GitHub Actions YAML, OIDC, environments/approvals, Azure DevOps templates, service connections. Write the list in your attempt.
hints: Be strict: 2 means you could answer the interview question without notes today.
Topics rated 0 become the first thing you do in their block.
steps.solution: There is no model answer: the list is yours. Review it with the instructor; topics at 0 or 1 get an extra exercise inside their block, and the gap list goes into the block feedback.

criteria.text: az, terraform, gh and git are installed and gh is signed in
criteria.how: Install the missing tool or run gh auth login, then run the automatic checks.

criteria.text: Azure CLI is signed in on a subscription that holds the platform state (rg-mfs-tfstate)
criteria.how: az login, then az account set --subscription <lab subscription>.

criteria.text: The state of 05-identity, 10-foundation and 20-governance is readable and their resource groups exist
criteria.how: Needs the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the state account (assigned by 00-bootstrap).

An attempt recorded for every exercise step
Gap list reviewed: every topic rated, the 0/1 topics turned into actions in blocks R2–R6
criteria.how: Paste the rated list as evidence and record the review.

criteria.text: English answer recorded (60–90 seconds)
Feedback recorded: technical, autonomy and English scores, gaps and next step

english.question: Walk me through the platform you operate: what is deployed today, how is it organised and what would you improve first?
followUps: What is only code and not deployed yet, and why?
english.modelAnswer: It's an Azure platform built with layered Terraform, one state file per layer so a change to identity can't break the network plan. Today the bootstrap, identity, foundation and governance layers are deployed: remote state with Entra-only access, OIDC identities for GitHub and Azure DevOps, a hub-and-spoke network with private DNS zones, and Azure Policy as code. Data, AKS, edge and observability are written but not deployed yet, to control cost. The first thing I'd improve is the CI login, which is failing on pull requests — that's my next fix.

blocks.next: Start R2 with the topics you rated 0 or 1 in networking and RBAC.

blocks.title: Azure: network, NSG, DNS, identity and RBAC
blocks.focus: Hub & spoke, NSG order, private DNS, control vs data plane
blocks.objective: Read the deployed hub & spoke like a reviewer: prove the peering, explain the NSG order and the private DNS links, and say who can read the Terraform state and why.
blocks.interviewAngle: "How does traffic reach your workload and how do you restrict it?" and "Owner can't read the blob — why?" are classic platform questions.

prerequisites.notes: Layer 10-foundation deployed (it is). Read-only: no command in this block changes Azure.

reuse.note: Same evidence as session C005 (peering, NSG, DNS links). C005 stays open until its own checker exists; the evidence you collect here is shown on it. Lab 20 (identities and permissions) needs its own sandbox and Validate.ps1.

recall.question: Is VNet peering transitive? If spoke A and spoke B both peer with the hub, can A reach B? What would you need?
recall.answer: No. Each peering is a pair of resources (one per side) and traffic does not hop through the hub. Spoke-to-spoke needs a direct peering or a router/firewall (Azure Firewall/NVA) in the hub with UDRs, or Virtual WAN.

recall.question: How does an NSG evaluate rules, and what is a service tag?
recall.answer: Lowest priority number first, first match wins, then the default rules (65000+). A service tag (AzureFrontDoor.Backend, Internet, VirtualNetwork) is a Microsoft-managed group of IP prefixes, so you don't maintain the list.

recall.question: How does a workload in the spoke resolve a private endpoint name such as myvault.vault.azure.net?
recall.answer: The public name has a CNAME to privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net. The private DNS zone privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net holds the A record with the private IP, and it must be linked to the VNet that asks (hub and spoke), otherwise the public IP is returned.

recall.question: Owner, Contributor and Storage Blob Data Contributor: which ones can read a blob when shared keys are disabled, and why?
recall.answer: Only a data-plane role (Storage Blob Data Reader/Contributor/Owner). Owner and Contributor are control plane (ARM): they manage the account and could list keys, but with shared keys disabled there is no key path, so they cannot read data without a data role.

steps.title: Prove the peering in both directions
steps.detail: A peering is two resources. Check both and say what Connected means.
steps.command:
az network vnet peering list -g rg-mfs-hub-lab --vnet-name vnet-mfs-hub-lab --query "[].{name:name, state:peeringState, remote:remoteVirtualNetwork.id}" -o table
az network vnet peering list -g rg-mfs-portal-lab --vnet-name vnet-mfs-portal-lab --query "[].{name:name, state:peeringState}" -o table
hints: What would you see if only one side existed?
Initiated means the other side is missing.
steps.solution: peer-hub-to-portal and peer-portal-to-hub, both Connected. If one side is deleted the other shows Disconnected (or Initiated while being created) and no traffic flows.

steps.title: Read the NSG in evaluation order
steps.detail: Sort the AKS NSG rules by priority and decide which rule handles (a) a request from Front Door to port 443, (b) a request from your home IP to port 80, (c) a request from any other Internet IP to port 443.
steps.command: az network nsg rule list -g rg-mfs-portal-lab --nsg-name nsg-mfs-aks-lab --query "sort_by([], &priority)[].{p:priority, name:name, access:access, src:sourceAddressPrefix, srcs:join(',', sourceAddressPrefixes), ports:join(',', destinationPortRanges)}" -o table
hints: First match wins, from the lowest number.
The operator rule uses sourceAddressPrefixes (a list), so sourceAddressPrefix is empty.
steps.solution: (a) 100 Allow-FrontDoor-Http (service tag AzureFrontDoor.Backend, 80/443). (b) 110 Allow-Operator-Http (your /32 from OPERATOR_IP_RANGES). (c) 4000 Deny-Internet-Http. Anything else falls to the default rules (65000 AllowVnetInBound, 65500 DenyAllInBound).

steps.title: Check the private DNS links
steps.detail: There are two private zones in the hub resource group. List them, then list the VNet links of each one yourself. The first command is given; write the second.
steps.command: az network private-dns zone list -g rg-mfs-hub-lab --query "[].name" -o tsv
hints: The command group is az network private-dns link vnet list.
It needs -g and -z (zone name).
steps.solution: az network private-dns link vnet list -g rg-mfs-hub-lab -z privatelink.database.windows.net -o table (and the same for privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net). Each zone has link-hub and link-portal, state Completed. Without link-portal, a pod in the spoke would resolve the public IP and the private endpoint would be bypassed (or blocked by the firewall).

steps.title: Who can read the Terraform state?
steps.detail: Get the id of the state storage account and list the role assignments on it. Identify each principal: you, the GitHub identity, the Azure DevOps identity.
steps.command:
$saId = az storage account list -g rg-mfs-tfstate --query "[0].id" -o tsv
az role assignment list --scope $saId ...
hints: Add a --query that projects principalName, principalType and roleDefinitionName.
Service principals show their app id or display name; compare with app-mfs-github-actions and app-mfs-azure-devops.
steps.solution: az role assignment list --scope $saId --query "[].{who:principalName, type:principalType, role:roleDefinitionName}" -o table → Storage Blob Data Contributor for your user (00-bootstrap state_operator) and for the GitHub and Azure DevOps service principals (05-identity pipelines_state). Your Owner role on the subscription is inherited and is control plane only.

steps.title: Describe the pipeline identities
steps.detail: No command given. Find the two app registrations created by 05-identity, their roles at subscription scope and the federated credentials of the GitHub one. Write what each identity may do.
hints: Display names start with app-mfs-.
az ad app list --display-name …, az role assignment list --assignee <appId> --all, az ad app federated-credential list --id <appId>.
steps.solution: app-mfs-github-actions and app-mfs-azure-devops. Each has subscription-scope roles from local.pipeline_role_pairs (see 05-identity) plus Storage Blob Data Contributor on the state account. The GitHub app has three federated credentials (pull_request, ref:refs/heads/main, environment:lab); the Azure DevOps app has one for the service connection. No client secret exists on either.

steps.title: Design-review trap (analysis, no change)
steps.detail: A teammate peers a second spoke (vnet-mfs-reporting) with the hub and says it can now call the portal API in your spoke on port 443. Using only the evidence you collected, prove or disprove it and say what you would add if the requirement is real.
hints: Is peering transitive?
Even with a route, which NSG rule would the traffic meet?
steps.solution: Disproved: peering is not transitive, so the reporting spoke has no path to the portal spoke through the hub. Watch the second trap: with a direct peering the reporting range becomes part of the VirtualNetwork service tag, the 4000 rule (source Internet) does not match and the default 65000 AllowVnetInBound lets it in — so restrict it with an explicit rule if that is not wanted. For a real requirement: direct peering or a hub firewall with UDRs, plus an explicit NSG rule for exactly that source and port.

criteria.text: Hub↔spoke peering is Connected in both directions
The AKS NSG has Front Door (100), operator IP (110) and deny Internet (4000) rules
Both private DNS zones are linked to the hub and spoke VNets
Your signed-in user has a Storage Blob Data role on the state account

An attempt recorded for every exercise step
Explained, with your own outputs: NSG decision for the three requests, why both DNS links are needed, and control vs data plane
English answer recorded (60–90 seconds)
Feedback recorded: technical, autonomy and English scores, gaps and next step

english.question: A security reviewer asks how traffic reaches your AKS subnet and how private DNS works in your hub-and-spoke network. Answer in 60 to 90 seconds.
followUps: Why can't an Owner read your state blob?
english.modelAnswer: The AKS subnet lives in a spoke VNet peered with the hub in both directions. Its NSG allows HTTP and HTTPS only from the Front Door service tag at priority 100 and from our operator IP at 110, and denies the Internet at 4000, so the only public entry is through Front Door and its WAF. Private endpoints resolve through private DNS zones in the hub — privatelink.database and privatelink.vaultcore — linked to both VNets, so the spoke gets the private IP. For access, we separate control plane and data plane: even an Owner can't read the state blob because shared keys are disabled; only identities with a Storage Blob Data role can.

blocks.next: Continue with R3: the same state account, now from Terraform's point of view.

blocks.title: Terraform: remote state, access, locking, plan and drift
blocks.focus: Backend, data-plane access, lease lock, plan reading, drift, recovery
blocks.objective: Show that the state is protected and recoverable, watch a lock happen, read a plan for drift and write a recovery runbook without executing it.
blocks.interviewAngle: "Where is your state, who can read it, how is it locked and how do you recover it?" — asked in almost every Terraform interview.

prerequisites.notes: Layers 00, 05, 10 and 20 deployed. Plans take a lease on the state blob (lock) but change no resource. The optional stale-lock exercise needs your explicit OK.

reuse.note: Same criteria as session C002 (state you can trust) plus a first look at drift (C004). Those sessions keep their own completion rules; the evidence collected here is shown on them.

recall.question: What is inside a Terraform state file and why is it sensitive?
recall.answer: The mapping from every resource address to the real object id, all attributes Terraform read (IPs, names, sometimes connection strings or keys), outputs and the serial/lineage. It can contain secrets in plain text, so access must be restricted and audited.

recall.question: How does the azurerm backend lock state, and what happens to a second apply at the same time?
recall.answer: It takes a lease on the state blob (infinite duration while running) and writes the lock info in the blob metadata. A second run fails with "Error acquiring the state lock" and shows the lock ID and who holds it.

recall.question: What is drift and how do you detect it without changing anything?
recall.answer: A difference between the real infrastructure and the code/state, usually from a manual change. Detect with terraform plan (refresh + compare) — in CI with -detailed-exitcode (0 = no changes, 2 = changes) on a schedule — never with apply.

recall.question: The state of one layer is corrupted. How do you recover it?
recall.answer: Back up the current blob (terraform state pull), find the last good version (blob versioning), promote it (copy that version over the current blob), run plan and confirm there is no unexpected change. Never hand-edit the JSON.

steps.title: Inspect the state account
steps.detail: Save the account name in $sa, then read the three settings that protect the state and the versioning setting of the blob service.
steps.command:
$sa = az storage account list -g rg-mfs-tfstate --query "[0].name" -o tsv
az storage account show -n $sa -g rg-mfs-tfstate --query "{sharedKey:allowSharedKeyAccess, publicBlob:allowBlobPublicAccess, tls:minimumTlsVersion}"
az storage account blob-service-properties show -n $sa -g rg-mfs-tfstate --query "{versioning:isVersioningEnabled, softDeleteDays:deleteRetentionPolicy.days}"
hints: Why does this read work even without a data-plane role?
Versioning is a property of the blob service, not of the container.
steps.solution: sharedKey false, publicBlob false, tls TLS1_2, versioning true, soft delete 7 days. These reads go through ARM (control plane), which is why your Owner role is enough for them.

steps.title: List state blobs and their versions
steps.detail: Now the data plane: list the blobs with Entra ID and include versions. Which layers have a blob and which one has the most versions?
steps.command: az storage blob list --account-name $sa -c tfstate --auth-mode login --include v --query "[].{name:name, version:versionId, current:isCurrentVersion}" -o table
hints: --auth-mode login forces Entra ID. A 403 means a missing data role, not a broken account.
Why is there no 00-bootstrap.tfstate?
steps.solution: 05-identity, 10-foundation and 20-governance blobs, several versions each (every apply writes one). No 00-bootstrap blob: it creates the storage, so it keeps local state (chicken and egg); it could be migrated later with terraform init -migrate-state.

steps.title: Watch the lock happen
steps.detail: Open a second terminal. In terminal B start the loop first, then in terminal A run a plan of 10-foundation. Watch the lease change and stop the loop with Ctrl+C. The plan only takes and releases a lease; it changes nothing.
steps.command:
# terminal B (start first)
while ($true) { az storage blob show --account-name $sa -c tfstate -n 10-foundation.tfstate --auth-mode login --query "{lease:properties.lease.state, duration:properties.lease.duration}" -o tsv; Start-Sleep 2 }
# terminal A
./scripts/azp.ps1 plan 10-foundation
hints: Which state does the lease show while the plan refreshes?
Where is the lock ID stored?
steps.solution: available → leased / infinite during the plan → available again. The lock ID and owner are written to the blob metadata (terraformlockid). A concurrent apply would fail with "Error acquiring the state lock".

steps.title: Read a plan for drift
steps.detail: Run the plan of 20-governance and read only the summary line. Decide: is there drift? If there is, which resource and is it expected? Paste the summary line in your attempt.
steps.command: ./scripts/azp.ps1 plan 20-governance
hints: "No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration." means no drift.
A change you did not code is drift; a change you did code and did not apply is pending work, not drift.
steps.solution: Expected after C001 and PR #14: no changes, or only the change you know is pending. In CI the same check is terraform plan -detailed-exitcode on a schedule (exit 2 = drift) — that is session C004.

steps.title: Write the recovery runbook (do not execute)
steps.detail: 20-governance.tfstate was overwritten with a broken file. Write the exact steps and commands to recover it, including how you prove the recovery worked.
hints: Start with a backup of what is there now.
The version list from the second step gives you the version id; az storage blob copy start accepts a source URI with ?versionid=.
steps.solution: 1) terraform -chdir=infra/terraform/20-governance state pull > backup.tfstate (after azp.ps1 init). 2) Find the last good versionId with the list from step 2. 3) az storage blob copy start --account-name $sa -c tfstate -b 20-governance.tfstate --auth-mode login --source-uri "https://$sa.blob.core.windows.net/tfstate/20-governance.tfstate?versionid=<id>". 4) ./scripts/azp.ps1 plan 20-governance → expect no unexpected changes. Never edit the JSON by hand; terraform state push of an older serial is rejected unless forced.

steps.title: Break/fix: the key that no longer works (read-only)
steps.detail: Run the listing with key authentication. Predict the result first, then explain the error and the right fix. This command only fails; it changes nothing. Optional, only with an explicit OK: close terminal A in the middle of a plan (close the window, not Ctrl+C) to leave a stale lock, then release it safely.
steps.command: az storage blob list --account-name $sa -c tfstate --auth-mode key -o table
hints: Which property did you read in the first step?
The account only accepts Entra ID.
steps.solution: "Key based authentication is not permitted on this storage account": allowSharedKeyAccess is false. The fix is --auth-mode login with a data role — never re-enabling shared keys. Stale lock: confirm nothing is running, then terraform -chdir=infra/terraform/10-foundation force-unlock <LockID> (or az storage blob lease break).

criteria.text: Shared key access is disabled on the state storage account
Blob versioning is enabled
State blobs exist for 05-identity, 10-foundation and 20-governance
At least one state blob has two or more versions
No state blob is left leased (no stale lock) at the end of the block
criteria.how: If a plan was interrupted, confirm nothing runs and release the lock with force-unlock.

criteria.text: Recall answers recorded before the instructions
An attempt recorded for every exercise step
Plan summary interpreted (drift or not, and why) and recovery runbook reviewed
English answer recorded (60–90 seconds)
Feedback recorded: technical, autonomy and English scores, gaps and next step

english.question: Where does your Terraform state live, who can read it, how is it locked and how would you recover it?
followUps: Why is the bootstrap layer on local state?
english.modelAnswer: Each layer has its own state blob in an Azure Storage account with shared keys and public access disabled, so the only way in is Entra ID with a Storage Blob Data role — that's me and the two pipeline identities, and every read is audited. During plan and apply Terraform takes a lease on the blob, so a second run fails to get the lock instead of corrupting the state. Versioning and soft delete are on: if a state gets corrupted I back up the current one, promote the last good version and run a plan to confirm nothing unexpected changes. Drift is caught by a scheduled plan with detailed exit codes.

blocks.next: Day 1 done. Day 2 starts with R4: the same plan, now run by GitHub Actions.

blocks.title: GitHub Actions: YAML, triggers, jobs, OIDC, environments and approvals
blocks.focus: Read the real workflow, then write one from a blank file
blocks.objective: Read the platform's infra workflow line by line, connect each job to the OIDC subject it presents, and write a plan/apply workflow from a blank file that passes the structural checks.
blocks.interviewAngle: "How do you deploy to Azure from GitHub Actions without secrets, and how do you stop an unreviewed apply?"

prerequisites.notes: gh signed in. The drill file is local and git-ignored (portal/.data/drills/), so nothing is pushed to the protected main.

reuse.note: Labs 09 (GitHub Actions build), 13 (environments and approvals), 21 (federated identity) and 04 (branch protection) cover the same ideas in their own sandbox: they are completed only by their Validate.ps1. Sessions C003 and C020 apply it to this platform.

recall.question: Which events trigger a workflow, and how do you restrict a pull_request trigger to changes under infra/?
recall.answer: on: push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch, schedule, workflow_call, etc. Restrict with paths: ['infra/**'] (and branches:) under the event.

recall.question: What does permissions: id-token: write do, and what does Entra check in that token?
recall.answer: It lets the job request an OIDC token from GitHub. Entra checks issuer (token.actions.githubusercontent.com), audience (api://AzureADTokenExchange) and subject (repo:<owner>/<repo>:<context>) against a federated credential of the app registration.

recall.question: What does an environment give you that a plain job does not?
recall.answer: Protection rules (required reviewers, wait timer, branch restrictions), environment secrets/variables, deployment history, and a different OIDC subject (repo:…:environment:<name>), so Azure can trust only gated jobs to apply.

recall.question: jobs, steps, needs and matrix: what does each do?
recall.answer: A job runs on its own runner; steps run in order inside it; needs makes a job wait for (and read outputs of) another; matrix fans one job out over values (e.g. one plan per layer).

steps.title: Read the real workflow
steps.detail: Open infra.yml and answer in your attempt: (1) which job runs on a pull request and which on a manual run; (2) where the approval happens; (3) which OIDC subject each job presents to Azure; (4) why the run job has a concurrency group. Then confirm the environment protection on GitHub.
steps.command:
Get-Content .github/workflows/infra.yml
gh api repos/edymonte/azure-enterprise-platform/environments --jq ".environments[] | {name, rules: [.protection_rules[].type]}"
hints: Look at the if: of each job and at environment:.
A job without environment presents the event context; a job with environment: lab presents environment:lab.
steps.solution: (1) plan runs on pull_request (matrix over four layers, read-only, -lock=false); run runs on workflow_dispatch. (2) environment: lab with required reviewers — the job waits for approval before any step runs. (3) plan presents repo:<repo>:pull_request; run presents repo:<repo>:environment:lab. (4) concurrency: tfstate-<layer> queues runs on the same layer instead of fighting for the state lock.

steps.title: Match subjects to federated credentials
steps.detail: List the federated credentials of the GitHub app registration and match each subject to the job that uses it. The client id is a repository variable; the second command is yours.
steps.command: $clientId = gh variable get AZURE_CLIENT_ID -R edymonte/azure-enterprise-platform
hints: az ad app federated-credential list --id $clientId
Project only the subject: --query "[].subject".

english.question: How do you deploy to Azure from GitHub Actions without storing a secret, and how do you stop an unreviewed apply?
followUps: What exactly does Azure compare in the token?
What happens to a plan running at the same time as an apply?
english.modelAnswer: We use OIDC. The workflow asks GitHub for a short-lived token with id-token: write, and Entra exchanges it for an Azure token because the app registration has a federated credential that trusts that issuer, audience and subject — for example pull requests for plan, and the lab environment for apply. There's no secret to leak or rotate. Pull requests only run a read-only plan; apply runs on a manual dispatch in a job bound to the lab environment, which has required reviewers, so nobody applies without an approval, and a concurrency group per layer queues runs on the same state.

blocks.focus: Read the real pipeline and template, then write one from a blank file
blocks.objective: Explain the platform's Azure Pipelines flow (Validate → Plan → Apply with approval), the template and the three kinds of variable syntax, and write a pipeline from a blank file that passes the structural checks.
blocks.interviewAngle: Azure DevOps shops ask about templates, variable groups, service connections with workload identity federation and approvals on environments.

prerequisites.notes: The drill is local. Reading the live organization (az400edilsonmontry) is optional and read-only; if it has no project for this platform yet, record that as an environment blocker, not as a mistake.

recall.question: Stage, job and deployment job: what does each add in Azure Pipelines?
recall.answer: A stage groups jobs and is the unit of approvals/conditions/dependsOn. A job runs steps on one agent. A deployment job targets an environment: it records deployments and honours the environment's approvals and checks, with strategies (runOnce, rolling, canary).

recall.question: ${{ }}, $( ) and $[ ]: when is each evaluated?
recall.answer: ${{ }} template expression, at compile time (parameters, template logic). $( ) macro, at runtime just before a task runs. $[ ] runtime expression, for variables and conditions evaluated at runtime (e.g. outputs of other jobs).

recall.question: What is a service connection with workload identity federation, and who authorizes a pipeline to use it?
recall.answer: An Azure Resource Manager connection whose service principal trusts the Azure DevOps issuer and a subject tied to that connection, so no secret is stored. A project admin creates it; each pipeline must be authorized (or the connection opened to all pipelines), and approvals/checks can be added on the connection itself.

recall.question: Where do approvals live in Azure DevOps?
recall.answer: On resources, not in YAML: environments, service connections, agent pools, variable groups, repos → Approvals and checks. A deployment job targeting the environment waits for them.

steps.title: Read the pipeline and the template

steps.title: Write a plan/apply pipeline from a blank file
steps.detail: Create portal/.data/drills/r5-infra-pipeline.yml without copying infra.yml. Requirements: a Plan stage and an Apply stage that depends on it; variables with a variable group; steps reused through a template with parameters; a service connection referenced by name or compile-time variable, never a secret; Apply as a deployment job on an environment. Save and run the automatic checks; then ask the instructor for the revisor-yaml review.
steps.command: code portal/.data/drills/r5-infra-pipeline.yml
hints: stages: - stage: Plan … - stage: Apply with dependsOn: Plan.
variables: - group: mfs-lab-common - name: serviceConnection value: sc-mfs-lab-wif
- deployment: apply / environment: mfs-lab / strategy: runOnce: deploy: steps: - template: templates/terraform-layer.yml
steps.solution:
trigger: none
pr:
  paths:
    include: [infra/*]
variables:
  - group: mfs-lab-common
  - name: serviceConnection
    value: sc-mfs-lab-wif
pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest
stages:
  - stage: Plan
    jobs:
      - job: plan
        steps:
          - template: templates/terraform-layer.yml
            parameters:
              layer: 10-foundation
              action: plan
              serviceConnection: ${{ variables.serviceConnection }}
  - stage: Apply
    dependsOn: Plan
    condition: and(succeeded(), ne(variables['Build.Reason'], 'PullRequest'))
    jobs:
      - deployment: apply
        environment: mfs-lab
        strategy:
          runOnce:
            deploy:
              steps:
                - checkout: self
                - template: templates/terraform-layer.yml
                  parameters:
                    layer: 10-foundation
                    action: apply
                    serviceConnection: ${{ variables.serviceConnection }}

english.question: Walk me through an Azure DevOps pipeline that plans on pull requests and applies with an approval. How does it authenticate, and how do you reuse it across layers?
followUps: Why must the service connection name be known at compile time?
Where do you configure the approval?
english.modelAnswer: The pipeline has three stages. Validate runs fmt and validate with no credentials. Plan runs a steps template with the layer as a parameter, so every layer reuses the same code. Apply is a deployment job on the mfs-lab environment, and it only runs on a manual run, never on a PR. The approval is configured on the environment under Approvals and checks, not in YAML. Authentication uses a service connection with workload identity federation, so there's no secret; AzureCLI hands the federated token to Terraform. The connection name is a compile-time value because Azure DevOps authorizes the pipeline to use it before the run starts.

recall.question: Without notes: list the stages a change goes through on this platform, from the feature branch to production.
recall.answer: Feature branch → PR with CI (lint, tests, build, scan) and required checks → squash merge to main → app pipeline builds and pushes the image once → opens a GitOps PR for dev → Argo CD syncs → PostSync smoke test → promotion PR to prod with the same image → sync + smoke. recall.question: Why does CI here open a pull request instead of deploying to the cluster?
recall.answer: GitOps (ADR-0003): Git is the source of truth and Argo CD pulls and applies, so every deploy is a reviewed commit, drift is corrected and rollback is a git revert. Pipelines never get cluster credentials.

recall.question: What does "build once, promote the same image" mean, and why does it matter?
recall.answer: The image built from main is the exact artifact promoted to every environment (ideally by digest, not by a mutable tag). What was tested in dev is what runs in prod; rebuilding per environment breaks that guarantee.

english.question: Walk me through your CI/CD: how does a change get from a developer's branch to production, in GitHub Actions and in Azure DevOps?
followUps: Why does the pipeline not deploy to the cluster?
english.modelAnswer: A developer opens a pull request; CI runs lint, tests, the build and a scan, and the checks are required before the squash merge. On main the pipeline builds the image once, pushes it to ACR and opens a pull request to the GitOps folder for dev. Argo CD syncs it and a smoke test runs after the sync. Promotion to production is another pull request with the same image. The pipelines never touch the cluster and never hold a secret: GitHub uses OIDC federated credentials and Azure DevOps a workload identity federation service connection, and applies wait for an environment approval. Rollback is a git revert. The same flow exists in both tools, so I can work with either team.

blocks.title: Kubernetes and AKS: API workloads, endpoints and troubleshooting
blocks.focus: Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, HTTP endpoints, AKS identities and diagnosis
blocks.objective: Trace a real customer-portal HTTP request through AKS, review the Terraform cluster and Helm design, and diagnose API failures from evidence without deploying anything as part of the exercise setup.
blocks.interviewAngle: How do you use APIs and endpoints? How does a request reach a Pod? How do you distinguish a REST endpoint, the Kubernetes API server and an Azure Private Endpoint? What do 404, 503 and ImagePullBackOff tell you?

prerequisites.notes: R4–R6 first. Source inspection and Helm rendering work without a cluster. A live kubectl observation requires previously approved AKS resources. The 40-aks Terraform layer is written but is not evidence of deployment; no apply or paid-resource creation is authorized by this block.

reuse.note: Uses the existing AKS layer and customer-portal workloads. Sessions retain their own checkers and live-cloud prerequisites; R7 creates no parallel lab.

recall.question: Without notes, distinguish Pod, Deployment, Service and Ingress. Trace GET /api/products from a user's browser to a Pod.
recall.answer: A Pod runs containers; a Deployment manages replicas and rollouts; a ClusterIP Service provides stable networking to selected ready Pods; an Ingress routes host/path HTTP(S) through an ingress controller. In this repo: Front Door (if edge is deployed) → ingress-nginx → Ingress /api → customer-portal-api Service → API Pod → GET /api/products.

recall.question: Explain an API, an HTTP endpoint such as GET /api/products, the Kubernetes API server endpoint and Azure Private Endpoint. Are these interchangeable?
recall.answer: An API is an interface/contract with operations. GET /api/products is one HTTP method + route. The Kubernetes API server endpoint manages the cluster through kubectl/controllers and Kubernetes RBAC. An Azure Private Endpoint is a private network interface/IP to a supported Azure service such as Key Vault or SQL. These solve different problems.

recall.question: Compare /healthz, /readyz and /api/products. Would HTTP 200 from /healthz prove the business API works? What happens when readiness returns 503?
recall.answer: /healthz is basic liveness; /readyz checks db.ping() and can return 503, causing the Pod to be excluded from ready Service endpoints without necessarily restarting it; /api/products tests the business/database route and can return 500. Liveness 200 alone does not prove business functionality.

recall.question: How does an AKS Pod access Key Vault without a stored secret? How does its OIDC issuer/subject differ from GitHub Actions OIDC?
recall.answer: The Pod uses a Kubernetes ServiceAccount token from the AKS OIDC issuer. A federated credential trusts issuer/audience/subject system:serviceaccount:namespace:name for a user-assigned managed identity, which exchanges that token for Entra access. GitHub Actions instead uses GitHub's issuer and repository/environment subject. Azure data-plane RBAC remains necessary.

steps.title: Inventory real API methods, endpoints and response contracts
steps.detail: Read the API source. For GET /healthz, /readyz, /api/info and /api/products, state purpose, successful HTTP status, possible failure and whether a liveness, readiness or smoke probe should call it.
steps.command: rg -n 'app.get|/healthz|/readyz|/api/' app/customer-portal/api/src/app.js
hints: Read each route handler; route names alone are insufficient.
Which handlers call db.ping or db.listProducts and what status do they return on error?
steps.solution: /healthz returns basic 200 liveness; /readyz checks the database and may return 503; /api/info returns service/version/environment information; /api/products returns business data or 500 if the data path fails. A smoke needs the business endpoint too.

steps.title: Trace Ingress → Service → Pod, then render Helm offline

helm template portal-dev gitops/charts/customer-portal -f gitops/envs/dev/platform.values.yaml -f gitops/envs/dev/values.yaml

steps.title: Inspect AKS, ACR, network and federated workload identity
steps.detail: Find Terraform configuration for AKS, node pools, ACR pull access, Kubernetes OIDC issuer, managed identity and federated ServiceAccount subjects. Separate Azure infrastructure ownership from Kubernetes GitOps ownership. Do not run terraform apply.
steps.command: rg -n 'kubernetes_cluster|node_pool|container_registry|AcrPull|oidc_issuer|workload_identity|federated_identity' infra/terraform/40-aks
hints: The kubelet identity needs ACR pull permissions; the application identity has different access.
Terraform configuration is not proof that the resource is deployed in Azure.
steps.solution: Terraform owns AKS, node pools, ACR, Azure RBAC, workload identity and federated credentials. GitOps owns Kubernetes desired state, including Deployments, Services, Ingress and NetworkPolicy. AKS ServiceAccount OIDC is distinct from the CI platform's federated identity.

steps.title: Write an evidence-first 404/503 and Pod-failure runbook
steps.detail: Scenario: GET /api/products returns 503 but /healthz works by Pod IP. Write Observation → Hypothesis → Read-only Test → Evidence for DNS/edge, Ingress, Service/EndpointSlices, ready Pods, API and database. Include ImagePullBackOff and CrashLoopBackOff branches. Do not run kubectl unless a cluster is authorized and running.
steps.command:
kubectl -n portal-dev get ingress,svc,endpoints,pods
kubectl -n portal-dev describe pod <pod-name>
kubectl -n portal-dev logs <pod-name> --previous
hints: A Service with no ready endpoints may generate upstream 503; trace the request hop by hop.
Use events for image pulls/scheduling, previous logs for restarts, and readiness for traffic eligibility.
steps.solution: Check the URL, DNS/edge, Ingress host/path and controller, Service selector/port, EndpointSlices, Deployment ready replicas, Pod events, logs, readiness and DB. A 404 suggests host/path/route; a 503 can mean no ready upstream or failing dependency. ImagePullBackOff: tag, AcrPull, network. CrashLoopBackOff: start error, probes, configuration, prior logs. Test rather than guessing from status alone.

steps.title: Explain HTTP API vs Kubernetes API server vs Azure Private Endpoint
steps.detail: For each endpoint, name its consumer, network path, identity/authorization and first diagnostic check for HTTP 401, 403 or a timeout. Explain the difference to a non-specialist client without confusing an application endpoint with Private Link.
hints: The AKS API server controls cluster resources; the application API serves users.
Private Endpoint is a private NIC and DNS path to a supported Azure service, not an HTTP route.
steps.solution: Application REST routes use HTTP methods and application authn/authz through Ingress. Kubernetes API server access uses control-plane connectivity and Kubernetes/Entra RBAC. Azure Private Endpoint maps private IP/DNS to an Azure resource, still requiring service-level authorization. A 401 suggests missing authentication, 403 authorization, and a timeout network/DNS/firewall, subject to actual evidence.

hints: Does the image tag/digest exist in ACR?

steps.solution: manifest unknown: verify tag/digest. unauthorized: inspect kubelet identity/AcrPull. timeout: inspect DNS/firewall/reachability. Collect events and registry evidence before changing anything.

recall.question: Why does app.yml open a GitOps PR instead of running kubectl apply? What happens when someone manually changes an Argo CD-managed Deployment?
recall.answer: The CI workflow builds, tests, scans and pushes an image, then proposes a desired-state change in Git. Argo CD pulls and reconciles that state, so CI needs no kubeconfig. With automated selfHeal, a manual edit that causes drift is reconciled back to the desired Git configuration.

recall.question: How do you prove prod runs the same tested image as dev? Why is an image digest stronger than a mutable tag?
recall.answer: Compare immutable image identities in dev/prod GitOps values and the running Pod imageID. The current workflow uses the Git SHA as a tag and copies it; immutable tags help, but a digest pins exact bytes even if tags could be moved. Never rebuild separately for prod.

recall.question: Can Argo CD be Synced/Healthy while GET /api/products fails? What evidence is different from /readyz and /api/info?
recall.answer: Yes. Synced means live Kubernetes resources match desired Git resources, not business correctness. Healthy reflects Kubernetes resource health; readiness marks which Pods receive traffic. /api/info can confirm version, while /api/products exercises the business/database API; both should be checked in a smoke test.

recall.question: The latest image causes CrashLoopBackOff in prod. Why is kubectl rollout undo not the durable rollback for an auto-sync GitOps application?
recall.answer: Git still declares the bad image; auto-sync/selfHeal may reapply it after an imperative rollback. Pause promotion, collect evidence, revert the GitOps deploy commit to a known-good image, approve/merge the revert and let Argo CD reconcile. Verify readiness and business API responses after recovery.

recall.question: When would you call a GitHub/Azure DevOps REST API rather than use the UI? How does an Azure DevOps service endpoint differ from an HTTP API endpoint? What do 401, 403 and 429 mean?
recall.answer: REST APIs are useful for scripted read-only run/PR inspection, evidence and integrations; use scoped authenticated requests and handle pagination/rate limits. An Azure DevOps service endpoint/service connection configures a trusted external service identity for a pipeline, not a business HTTP route. 401 means authentication missing/invalid, 403 permission denied, and 429 rate limited; inspect response headers and retry-after/backoff safely.

steps.title: Map commit → tests → scan → ACR → GitOps PR → Argo CD
steps.detail: Read the real app workflow and portal-dev Application. Identify the trigger, OIDC trust, image tag, scan, ACR push, dev deploy PR, Argo CD source and cluster boundary. State which process actually contacts Kubernetes. Explain when a read-only GitHub/Azure DevOps API call is useful for pipeline evidence, versus an Azure DevOps service connection that grants pipeline access to Azure.
steps.command:
Get-Content .github/workflows/app.yml
Get-Content gitops/apps/portal-dev.yaml
hints: Find the create-pull-request step that edits gitops/envs/dev/values.yaml.
The Argo CD Application tracks the Git repository; the app workflow contains no kubectl apply.
steps.solution: After merge to main, app.yml tests, authenticates to Azure via OIDC, builds and scans images, pushes them to ACR and opens a PR updating dev image tags. The reviewed GitOps merge lets Argo CD sync to AKS. A separate promotion PR copies the tested tag to prod values. CI does not need cluster credentials.

steps.title: Compare DEV/PROD Helm renders and Argo CD Applications
steps.detail: Compare the two values files and Argo CD Applications. Render each chart offline, locate namespace, desired image, syncPolicy, prune/selfHeal and the PostSync smoke Job. Predict whether a manual kubectl edit persists.
steps.command:
helm template portal-dev gitops/charts/customer-portal -f gitops/envs/dev/platform.values.yaml -f gitops/envs/dev/values.yaml
helm template portal-prod gitops/charts/customer-portal -f gitops/envs/prod/platform.values.yaml -f gitops/envs/prod/values.yaml
hints: Read gitops/apps/portal-dev.yaml and portal-prod.yaml; what does automated selfHeal do?
A successful Helm render is only static evidence, not proof of Argo CD Synced/Healthy.
steps.solution: Applications track main and render environment-specific values. Automated sync/selfHeal reconciles drift and prune removes deleted resources where configured. Check namespace, image tag and rendered smoke hooks. Static rendering does not establish that the cluster or Application is running.

steps.title: Design an API and endpoint smoke-test contract
steps.detail: Define expected HTTP methods, status codes and response fields for GET /healthz, /readyz, /api/info and /api/products. Explain GET versus mutating POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE, bearer-token handling, 401/403/404/429/5xx diagnosis, timeouts and safe retries. Compare the in-cluster PostSync test with smoke.yml through public DNS/Front Door. Explain why a healthy Pod might still expose a broken business API.
steps.command:
Get-Content gitops/charts/customer-portal/templates/smoke-test.yaml
Get-Content .github/workflows/smoke.yml
hints: The version in /api/info should match the image promoted from dev.
The in-cluster job can succeed while the public ingress/edge path fails; these are different verification boundaries.
steps.solution: Record HTTP method, URL, response status/body, expected image SHA and timestamp. Check /healthz for process liveness, /readyz for dependency readiness, /api/info for version and /api/products for the real data path. PostSync exercises an in-cluster route; public smoke additionally depends on DNS, Front Door and Ingress when the edge is deployed.

steps.title: Write the application GitOps delivery workflow from a blank file
steps.detail: In the ignored drills directory, author a local YAML from memory: path-filtered trigger, minimal permissions/OIDC, checkout, tests/build/scan, ACR push, reviewed dev GitOps PR and a distinct prod promotion PR. Save your attempt before consulting app.yml or opening the solution. Do not run the workflow or deploy.
steps.command: New-Item -ItemType File -Force portal/.data/drills/r8-app-gitops.yml
hints: Start with on, permissions, jobs and checkout. Separate CI artifact creation from CD desired-state changes.
Deploy through a reviewed GitOps change; CI does not need Kubernetes credentials.
steps.solution: Reference structure: push main only when app/** changes; workflow_dispatch promotion input; id-token:write and scoped contents/pull-requests permissions; checkout, tests, azure/login with federated repo vars, Docker build, Trivy scan, ACR push, create-pull-request changing dev values; promotion copies the same immutable image identity to prod values via a separate PR. Never run kubectl apply. Verify approval and PR-trigger behavior before live use.

steps.title: P1 incident: Argo CD Synced, API Pods crashing
steps.detail: Simulated production failure: a new release is Synced but its API Pods enter CrashLoopBackOff. Write Observation → Hypothesis → Read-only Test → Evidence → Containment → Git revert → Smoke verification → Prevention. Include a timeline, the approval boundary and an English customer update. Do not inject faults.
steps.command:
kubectl -n portal-prod get deployment,pods,svc,endpoints
kubectl -n portal-prod describe pod <pod-name>
kubectl -n portal-prod logs <pod-name> --previous
hints: Synced is desired-state parity, not proof that the API is healthy.
Revert the bad GitOps deploy commit rather than only changing the live Deployment. Confirm /api/products after recovery.
steps.solution: Stop promotion; capture the failed image SHA, CI and GitOps PR, Argo sync/health, Pod events, previous logs, readiness and /api/products status. Revert the deploy PR to the last known good image through Git, with production review; let Argo CD sync. Validate ready replicas, /api/info version and the business-route response, then record time to restore, root cause and prevention gate.

english.question: Your GitOps release is Synced, but customers get errors from the API. How would you prove which endpoint failed, restore service through Argo CD and prevent recurrence?
followUps: Why does CI change Git instead of deploying directly to AKS?
How can Argo CD be Synced while the business endpoint fails?
How do you prove prod runs the exact image tested in dev?
How would you diagnose an API call that gets 401, 403 or 429, and when would you use a service connection instead?
english.modelAnswer: I would first correlate the release commit, image SHA and pipeline run with the failing HTTP endpoint. Next I would compare GitOps desired state with the Argo CD Application and the Deployment, then inspect Pod events, readiness and logs and run the business-route smoke test. Synced means Kubernetes resources match Git, but it does not guarantee that /api/products works. If the release is responsible, I would revert its GitOps deploy commit to the last known good immutable image, let Argo CD reconcile and verify ready Pods, /api/info version and a successful /api/products response. I would document root cause, recovery time and the missing test or approval gate.
